subject: Geography
source: AQA GCSE Geography (8035) spec; adapted from school Drive lesson plans (Y10 Global Atmospheric Circulation, Desert Opportunities, 7.6 Reducing the Risks of Desertification) and the Y10 KS4 curriculum map; Geog GCSE AQA folder (3.1 Global Atmospheric Circulation, 3.2 Where are Storms Formed)

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Weather hazards (AQA 3.1.1 The challenge of natural hazards)
lessons.title: Global atmospheric circulation
objectives: Identify the Hadley, Ferrel and Polar cells on a circulation diagram
Explain where air rises and sinks and why this creates high and low pressure
Link pressure belts to wet and dry climates around the world

keywords.def: the large-scale movement of air around the Earth that moves heat from the Equator towards the poles
the circulation cell between the Equator and about 30 degrees north and south
the middle cell, between about 30 and 60 degrees north and south
the cell between about 60 degrees and the poles
an area where air is rising, often bringing cloud and rain
an area where air is sinking, often bringing dry, clear weather

starter: Say Bismillah. Define weather and define climate.
Name two places on Earth that are very hot. Which one is wet and which is dry?
What happens to warm air: does it rise or sink?

teach.heading: Why does the Earth need circulation?
bullets: The Sun heats the Equator most strongly because rays are concentrated there.
The poles receive less heat because rays are spread over a larger area.
Air movement carries heat from the Equator towards the poles.
teach.note: Misconception to correct: the Equator is not hot because it is closer to the Sun. The difference in distance is tiny. The same amount of energy is concentrated on a small area at the Equator but spread over a large, curved area near the poles. Use a torch on a globe or a ball held at different angles. Ask: if heat only stayed where it landed, what would the Equator and poles be like?

teach.heading: The three cells
bullets: Hadley cell: Equator to 30 degrees north and south.
Ferrel cell: 30 to 60 degrees north and south.
Polar cell: 60 degrees to the poles.
teach.note: Draw the diagram live and build it one cell at a time. Pupils must be able to reproduce and label it in an exam. Make the point that the three cells are connected like gears: the Hadley and Polar cells are driven by heating and cooling, and the Ferrel cell is driven by the other two. Check pupils can say north AND south because the pattern is mirrored.

teach.heading: Rising air and low pressure
bullets: At the Equator, hot air rises and leaves low pressure at the surface.
Rising air cools, water vapour condenses, clouds form and heavy rain falls.
At about 60 degrees, warm and cold air meet and rise again.
teach.note: Chain of reasoning for the 4-6 mark questions: heating, air rises, pressure at the surface falls, air cools as it rises, condensation, cloud, rainfall. Link to tropical rainforests (Amazon, Congo, Indonesia). Link 60 degrees north to the UK: unsettled, wet weather because the UK sits near this rising air. Misconception: low pressure does not mean cold; it means rising air.

teach.heading: Sinking air and high pressure
bullets: At about 30 degrees, cool air sinks, creating high pressure.
Sinking air warms and holds moisture, so skies are clear and dry.
At the poles, cold air sinks, giving cold, dry conditions.
teach.note: This is where the great hot deserts are found: Sahara, Arabian, Thar, Kalahari and Australian deserts are all close to 30 degrees north or south. Ask pupils to find these on a world map. Key correction: not every place at 30 degrees is a desert, because local factors such as mountains and ocean currents also affect climate. Link forward to lessons 5 to 8 on hot deserts.

teach.heading: Surface winds
bullets: Air moves at the surface from high pressure to low pressure.
Trade winds blow towards the Equator; westerlies blow towards 60 degrees.
The Earth's rotation bends winds, so they are not straight north or south.
teach.note: Keep this light for the first lesson: pupils need to know that wind is air moving from high to low pressure, and that the UK's prevailing wind is the south-westerly, bringing moist air from the Atlantic. The bending of winds (Coriolis effect) will return in lesson 2 for tropical storms. Ask: why are the UK's winters mild and wet compared with the same latitude in Canada?

practice: On a blank diagram, label the Equator, 30 degrees, 60 degrees and the poles, then mark where air rises (R) and sinks (S).
Complete the sentence: At 30 degrees north, air _____ so pressure is _____ and the weather is usually _____.
independent: Explain why tropical rainforests are found close to the Equator. Use the words rising, cooling, condensation and low pressure. (4 marks)
Explain why many hot deserts are found near 30 degrees north and south of the Equator. (4 marks)
Stretch: Explain why the UK has more unsettled weather than the Sahara. (6 marks)
exit: At which latitude does air rise to create low pressure, 0, 30 or 90 degrees?
In one sentence, explain why high pressure usually brings dry weather.
lessons.homework: Redraw the three-cell diagram from memory, label it, and write three sentences linking it to rainforests and deserts.
lessons.send: SEND: pre-labelled diagram with cut-out arrows to place. EAL: sentence frames 'Air rises at ... so ...'. Stretch: explain why the cells do not meet exactly at 30 and 60 degrees every day of the year.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Weather hazards (AQA 3.1.1 The challenge of natural hazards)
lessons.title: Tropical storms: distribution and formation
objectives: Describe the global distribution of tropical storms
State the conditions needed for a tropical storm to form
Explain the sequence of formation and why storms weaken over land

keywords.def: an intense low-pressure weather system with very strong winds and heavy rain that forms over warm tropical oceans
regional names for a tropical storm: Atlantic, north-west Pacific and Indian Ocean
the way the Earth's rotation bends moving air, causing tropical storms to spin
the change of water from liquid to water vapour
a rise in sea level caused by a storm's low pressure and strong winds

starter: Say Bismillah. Where does air rise to create low pressure: at 0, 30 or 90 degrees?
What happens to water vapour when rising air cools?
What is the difference between weather and climate?

teach.heading: Where do tropical storms occur?
bullets: Between about 5 and 30 degrees north and south of the Equator.
Over warm oceans such as the Caribbean, Bay of Bengal and western Pacific.
They do not form right on the Equator.
teach.note: Show a world map of storm tracks. Pupils should describe the pattern with directions and latitudes. Give the three names: hurricanes in the Atlantic and north-east Pacific, typhoons in the north-west Pacific (including the Philippines), cyclones in the Indian Ocean and South Pacific. It is the same type of storm. Ask: why are there almost none on the south Atlantic coast of Brazil?

teach.heading: Conditions needed
bullets: Sea surface temperature of at least 27 degrees Celsius.
Warm water to a depth of about 50 metres.
Far enough from the Equator for the Earth's rotation to spin the storm.
teach.note: Pupils need to learn these three conditions precisely. Common error: saying the sea must be 'hot' with no figure. Also, there must be little wind shear for the storm to build upwards, but you may mention this only for stretch. Explain the 5 degree limit: near the Equator the Coriolis effect is too weak to make air spin.

teach.heading: How a tropical storm forms
bullets: Warm seas evaporate; moist air rises, cools and condenses into huge clouds.
Condensation releases heat, driving more air to rise rapidly.
Low pressure draws in air at the surface and the storm spins.
teach.note: Draw a four-step sequence: evaporation, rising and condensation, release of heat energy, inward rush of air then spinning because of the Coriolis effect. Pupils often write 'the storm gets hotter'. Correct them: the heat released by condensation is the fuel. Ask pupils to explain in their own words why a storm needs warm water.

teach.heading: Movement and decline
bullets: Storms are steered westwards by the trade winds.
They curve away from the Equator as the Earth rotates.
Over land or cold water they lose their energy supply and weaken.
teach.note: Link back to the surface winds in lesson 1. The key explanation of weakening: no more warm water means no more evaporation, no heat is released, and friction with land slows the winds. Land weakens the winds, but the rain can still cause severe flooding inland. Ask pupils why coastal areas are hit hardest.

teach.heading: Tropical storms and climate change
bullets: Warmer oceans could make storms more intense, with stronger winds.
Sea level rise makes storm surges more dangerous.
Scientists are less sure the number of storms will increase.
teach.note: Be careful and balanced here. Evidence supports the idea that warmer seas give more energy and heavier rainfall, and that sea level rise worsens flooding. Total numbers are less certain. Encourage evidence-based language: 'could', 'may', 'is likely to'.

practice: Describe the distribution of tropical storms shown on the map (use latitude and ocean names). (3 marks)
Put these formation steps in order: air spins; water evaporates; condensation releases heat; warm air rises; low pressure draws in air.
independent: Explain why tropical storms form over oceans between 5 and 30 degrees north and south. (4 marks)
Explain why tropical storms lose strength when they reach land. (3 marks)
Stretch: Explain how climate change might affect the danger from tropical storms. (6 marks)
exit: State the minimum sea temperature needed for a tropical storm to form.
Give one reason why tropical storms do not form on the Equator.
lessons.homework: Draw an annotated diagram of how a tropical storm forms, with at least six labels.
lessons.send: SEND: sequencing cards for formation. EAL: highlight command words; word bank for evaporate, condense, rotate. Stretch: research the latitudes of two real storms and explain their paths.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Weather hazards (AQA 3.1.1 The challenge of natural hazards)
lessons.title: Typhoon Haiyan: structure and effects
objectives: Describe the structure of a tropical storm including the eye and eye wall
Describe the primary and secondary effects of Typhoon Haiyan (2013)
Outline immediate and long-term responses and compare them

keywords.def: the calm centre of a tropical storm where air sinks and skies are often clear
the ring of towering clouds around the eye with the strongest winds and heaviest rain
the direct, immediate damage caused by a hazard
knock-on problems that follow, such as disease or loss of jobs
actions taken in the hours and days after a disaster, such as rescue and emergency aid
actions taken in the following months and years, such as rebuilding

starter: Say Bismillah. State two conditions needed for a tropical storm to form.
What is the name for a tropical storm in the north-west Pacific?
Define primary effects and secondary effects of a natural hazard.

teach.heading: Structure of a tropical storm
bullets: The eye is 30 to 50 km wide: sinking air, light winds, few clouds.
The eye wall has the strongest winds and torrential rain.
Cloud bands spiral outward; the whole storm can be hundreds of kilometres wide.
teach.note: Draw a cross-section. Emphasise that air sinks in the eye, which is why it is calm and often clear, but rises rapidly in the eye wall. A frequent misconception is that the eye is the most dangerous part; the eye wall is. People who think the storm has passed when the eye arrives can be caught out by the second half. Wind speed must reach about 119 km/h to be classed as a hurricane or typhoon.

teach.heading: Case study: Typhoon Haiyan, 2013
bullets: Struck the Philippines on 8 November 2013 with winds over 300 km/h.
Philippines is a newly emerging economy (NEE) with many people on the coast.
Storm surge in Tacloban reached several metres, flooding coastal areas.
teach.note: Locate the Philippines on a map, between the Pacific and the South China Sea; lots of islands, many low-lying coastal communities and poor-quality housing. The typhoon made landfall in the central Philippines (Leyte and Samar). Wind speeds were among the strongest ever recorded at landfall. Keep figures approximate: over 6,000 deaths, about four million displaced, over one million homes damaged. Stress the human side with compassion.

teach.heading: Primary and secondary effects
bullets: Primary: over 6,000 people died; over 1 million homes damaged or destroyed.
Primary: roads, airports and power lines were destroyed.
Secondary: food and clean water shortages, disease, and loss of livelihoods.
teach.note: Ask pupils to classify further effects as primary or secondary: crops destroyed (primary, farmers' livelihoods lost then secondary), looting (secondary), people homeless (primary/secondary depending on explanation). Include environmental effects: coconut plantations and mangroves destroyed. Make sure pupils use figures from the case study; examiners reward place-specific detail.

teach.heading: Immediate and long-term responses
bullets: Immediate: international aid, rescue, food, water and temporary shelter.
Immediate: damaged roads and airports slowed the delivery of aid.
Long-term: rebuilding homes, replanting mangroves, better shelters and warning.
teach.note: Many countries and charities sent aid, including Muslim charities. Ask pupils: why was getting aid to remote islands so hard? Long-term: 'build back better' by constructing stronger homes further from the coast, reinforcing storm shelters, and restoring mangroves that act as natural barriers. Compare an NEE with a wealthy country: more reliance on overseas aid. Do not overstate; keep to widely reported actions.

practice: Label a diagram of a tropical storm: eye, eye wall, rising air, sinking air, spiralling cloud.
Complete a table with columns Primary / Secondary / Immediate / Long-term for Typhoon Haiyan using three facts each.
independent: Describe the structure of a tropical storm. (3 marks)
Using a named tropical storm, explain its primary and secondary effects. (6 marks)
Stretch: Assess the importance of immediate responses compared with long-term responses after Haiyan. (6 marks)
exit: Which part of a tropical storm has the strongest winds: the eye or the eye wall?
Give one secondary effect of Typhoon Haiyan.
lessons.homework: Write a 150-word news report on Haiyan using at least four facts and one human impact.
lessons.send: SEND: case study fact-sheet with highlighted facts. EAL: key words with pictures. Stretch: compare Haiyan with a tropical storm that hit a high-income country.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Weather hazards (AQA 3.1.1 The challenge of natural hazards)
lessons.title: Reducing the effects of tropical storms
objectives: Describe how monitoring, prediction, protection and planning reduce risk
Explain how each strategy saves lives or reduces damage
Evaluate which strategies are most effective in a country such as the Philippines

keywords.def: tracking a hazard using tools such as satellites, radar and weather stations
forecasting where and when a hazard will strike and how strong it will be
actions that reduce damage, such as strong buildings and sea defences
preparing people and land use before a hazard, including evacuation routes and drills
a coastal tree that grows in salt water and reduces wave and surge energy

starter: Say Bismillah. Name the two parts of a tropical storm's structure and what each is like.
Give one primary effect and one secondary effect of Typhoon Haiyan.
What is meant by an immediate response?

teach.heading: Four ways to manage risk
bullets: Monitoring: satellites, aircraft and radar track storms.
Prediction: forecasts give the path, strength and landfall time.
Protection: buildings and defences resist wind, flood and surge.
Planning: evacuation routes, drills, education and land-use zoning.
teach.note: Introduce the acronym MPPP or the four words in order. Ask pupils which is cheapest (planning, education) and which is expensive (sea walls, strong buildings). Note: these are the same four ideas used for tectonic hazards, so pupils can transfer knowledge. Ask pupils which strategies need money and technology and which can work in a poorer country.

teach.heading: Monitoring and prediction
bullets: Satellites show storm position and size; planes fly into the storm for data.
Forecasts are issued days ahead so people can leave.
Predictions have limits: the exact path and strength can still change.
teach.note: Explain the 'cone of uncertainty' on a forecast map. Accuracy has improved because of satellites and supercomputers. Limitation: forecasting rapid strengthening is harder. A good evaluation point: warnings only save lives if people receive them, understand them, and have somewhere safe to go. Mention text alerts and local radio.

teach.heading: Protection and planning
bullets: Strong buildings: reinforced roofs and stilts keep homes above floods.
Cyclone shelters and sea walls protect people on the coast.
Mangroves and drills reduce damage and speed up evacuation.
teach.note: Compare cost: mangrove restoration is low cost and environmentally friendly; sea walls are expensive. Land-use planning means keeping essential buildings away from the shore. In a poorer country, community training and low-cost techniques are more realistic. Link to the Philippines after Haiyan: shelters, early warning, relocation inland, mangrove replanting.

teach.heading: Which strategy is best?
bullets: Prediction saves lives only if people can act on warnings.
Protection reduces damage but is costly for poorer countries.
A combination of strategies is usually most effective.
teach.note: Model an evaluative paragraph: Point (monitoring is effective), Evidence (e.g. forecasts allowed evacuations), Explanation, then a counter-point and judgement. Teach pupils to finish with a clear, justified decision, not 'it depends'. This builds the 6-mark skills needed for AQA.

practice: Match each strategy to its example: monitoring, prediction, protection, planning, with the examples satellites, forecasts, sea walls, evacuation drills.
Write a Point-Evidence-Explain paragraph on why forecasts save lives.
independent: Explain how planning and preparation can reduce the effects of a tropical storm. (4 marks)
'Protection is the most effective way to reduce the impact of tropical storms.' To what extent do you agree? (6 marks)
Stretch: Design a low-cost storm-safety plan for a coastal village in the Philippines and justify three choices.
exit: Give one reason why a poorer country may struggle to build sea walls.
lessons.homework: Create a one-page storm preparation leaflet for a family living on a coast, using the four strategies.
lessons.send: SEND: sentence starters for the 6-mark evaluation. EAL: bilingual glossary. Stretch: research how Bangladesh cyclone shelters reduced deaths.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Hot desert environments (AQA 3.1.2 The living world)
lessons.title: Hot deserts: climate, location and adaptations
objectives: Locate the world's main hot deserts and describe their climate
Explain why hot deserts occur at about 30 degrees north and south
Describe how plants and animals adapt to desert conditions

keywords.def: a dry area with less than 250 mm of rain a year and very high daytime temperatures
the difference between the highest daytime and lowest night-time temperature
a feature that helps a plant or animal survive in its environment
active at night rather than during the day
a plant adapted to survive in very dry conditions

starter: Say Bismillah. At what latitude does air sink to create high pressure?
Why does sinking air bring dry weather?
Name two hot deserts you know.

teach.heading: Where are hot deserts?
bullets: Found around 15 to 30 degrees north and south of the Equator.
Examples: Sahara, Arabian, Thar, Kalahari, Great Victoria.
Many are in the centre or west of continents.
teach.note: Use a world map with the Tropics marked. Pupils should link directly to lesson 1: sinking air at about 30 degrees means high pressure and clear skies. Add the local factors: distance from the sea, rain-shadow effects and cold ocean currents, such as in the Namib. The Arabian Peninsula is relevant for pupils' own knowledge; the Rub' al-Khali is one of the largest sand deserts in the world.

teach.heading: Desert climate
bullets: Very low rainfall: under 250 mm a year, and unreliable.
Daytime temperatures often above 40 degrees Celsius.
Clear skies cause big falls at night, so the diurnal range is large.
teach.note: Use a climate graph of a hot desert (e.g. Cairo or a Sahara site). Pupils practise describing a climate graph: state rainfall total, highest and lowest temperatures, and use units. Explain the large diurnal range: no cloud, so heat escapes quickly at night, and the dry air holds little heat. Misconception: deserts are not always sand; many are rocky or stony.

teach.heading: Plant adaptations
bullets: Cacti store water in thick stems.
Spines instead of leaves reduce water loss.
Long or wide roots reach water deep down or after rainfall.
teach.note: Ask for 'feature then function' explanations: the waxy skin reduces water loss because it limits evaporation. Introduce the word adaptation as a feature that helps survival. Some seeds lie dormant for years until rain comes, then bloom quickly. Pupils should give two or three adaptations with a reason for each, as in an exam.

teach.heading: Animal adaptations
bullets: Camel: stores fat in its hump and has wide feet for sand.
Fennec fox: large ears lose heat; pale fur reflects the Sun.
Many animals are nocturnal or burrow to avoid the heat.
teach.note: Camels do not store water in their humps; they store fat. This is a very common misconception. Camels can also tolerate large changes in body temperature and drink large amounts quickly. The kangaroo rat gets water from seeds. Link Arabian camel and Bedouin knowledge for context and note that Allah has equipped creation for each environment; a good moment for reflection without pressing doctrine.

practice: Describe the location of the Sahara Desert using the latitude lines on the map. (2 marks)
Complete a table: adaptation, plant or animal, and how it helps survival, for cactus, camel and fennec fox.
independent: Explain why hot deserts are found around 30 degrees north and south. (4 marks)
Describe the climate shown on the climate graph for a hot desert. (3 marks)
Stretch: Explain how the structure of a cactus reflects the climate it lives in. (4 marks)
exit: State the maximum annual rainfall of a hot desert.
Explain one way a camel is adapted to the desert.
lessons.homework: Draw and annotate one desert plant and one desert animal showing at least three adaptations.
lessons.send: SEND: adaptation matching cards. EAL: picture glossary. Stretch: explain why the Atacama is so dry despite not being at 30 degrees in the same way as the Sahara.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Hot desert environments (AQA 3.1.2 The living world)
lessons.title: Hot desert opportunities and challenges: the Thar Desert
objectives: Locate the Thar Desert and describe its main features
Describe opportunities for development in the Thar Desert
Explain the challenges of extreme temperatures and water supply

keywords.def: a chance to develop economically, such as through mining or farming
a difficulty that limits development, such as extreme heat or lack of water
supplying water to land using canals, pipes or sprinklers to grow crops
underground rock that stores water
how easy it is to reach and travel around a place
a small earth-dam that traps rainwater, used in Rajasthan

starter: Say Bismillah. Name two ways plants or animals adapt to desert conditions.
What is the rainfall total that defines a hot desert?
Name a desert in Asia.

teach.heading: Where is the Thar Desert?
bullets: In north-west India (mainly Rajasthan) and eastern Pakistan.
India's Thar is one of the world's most heavily populated deserts.
Hot summers; low, unreliable rainfall; sand dunes and rocky plains.
teach.note: Locate it on a map with the Indus plain and the Aravalli hills. Ask pupils why more people live here than in the Sahara. Describe climate: summer temperatures often above 45 degrees Celsius; a monsoon influence brings some rain between July and September but it is unreliable. Key point: the Thar is the case study for AQA hot desert development in this course.

teach.heading: Opportunities for development
bullets: Mining: minerals such as gypsum, limestone and sandstone.
Energy: large solar farms in the strong, reliable sunshine.
Tourism: camel safaris and historic cities like Jaisalmer.
teach.note: Link each opportunity to a physical feature of the desert: solar farms use clear skies and flat land; tourism uses unique landscape and culture; farming uses irrigation. Mention the Indira Gandhi Canal, which brings water from the Himalayan rivers over hundreds of kilometres and has allowed crops such as wheat and cotton to be grown. Ask pupils which opportunity creates most jobs.

teach.heading: Challenge: extreme temperatures
bullets: Heat above 45 degrees Celsius makes outdoor work dangerous.
Evaporation is high, so water is lost quickly from soil and reservoirs.
Heat limits farming and tourism in summer.
teach.note: Ask pupils to think of workers and tourists: heat stroke risk, extra cost of cooling buildings, crops wilting. Ask: how does heat make the water challenge worse? Pupils should make a link between evaporation and water supply. A strong answer connects temperature to its human impact.

teach.heading: Challenge: water supply and accessibility
bullets: Rain is low and unreliable; groundwater in aquifers is being used up.
Johads and canals help, but supplies are limited.
Remote areas have poor roads, so building and tourism are harder.
teach.note: Sources of water: rainfall collected in johads, canals such as the Indira Gandhi Canal, and wells that reach aquifers. Falling water tables mean wells have to go deeper. Accessibility: loose sand and long distances make roads and pipelines expensive. Make sure pupils see that each opportunity is limited by a challenge.

teach.heading: Balancing the two
bullets: Population growth increases demand for water and food.
Climate change may make rainfall less predictable.
Development must be sustainable to protect people and land.
teach.note: Ask: is it right to develop a fragile desert? Use the 'opportunity, challenge, judgement' approach. Link to stewardship: the Qur'an teaches that we are khalifah on Earth (2:30) and should not cause corruption on it after it has been set in order (7:56). This leads naturally into lessons 7 and 8 on desertification.

practice: Complete an opportunity/challenge table for the Thar using at least three of each.
Explain how the Indira Gandhi Canal has helped farming in the Thar.
independent: Explain two opportunities for economic development in a hot desert. (4 marks)
Explain why extreme temperatures are a challenge for development in hot deserts. (3 marks)
Stretch: 'The opportunities of developing hot deserts outweigh the challenges.' Discuss using the Thar. (6 marks)
exit: Name one mineral or resource that can be developed in the Thar.
Give one reason why water supply is a challenge in the Thar.
lessons.homework: Write a 6-mark answer to: 'Explain the challenges of developing a hot desert environment.'
lessons.send: SEND: model answer with missing words and a fact bank. EAL: sentence starters. Stretch: compare the Thar with another hot desert such as the Sahara.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Hot desert environments (AQA 3.1.2 The living world)
lessons.title: Causes of desertification
objectives: Define desertification and locate areas at risk, such as the Sahel
Explain natural and human causes of desertification
Explain how soil erosion makes the problem worse

keywords.def: the process by which land becomes degraded and turns into desert
a semi-arid belt of land south of the Sahara across Africa
when too many animals eat the vegetation, leaving soil bare
growing crops too often so soil nutrients are used up
the removal of topsoil by wind or water
a place that is easily damaged by human activity

starter: Say Bismillah. What is the rainfall range for a hot desert?
Name one challenge of living in the Thar Desert.
What is soil erosion?

teach.heading: What is desertification?
bullets: Land on desert edges loses its vegetation and topsoil.
It affects semi-arid areas such as the Sahel in Africa.
Millions of people lose farmland, food and income.
teach.note: Show a map of the Sahel and the areas of Africa most at risk, plus other regions such as Central Asia and north-west India. Explain that desertification is not the desert 'spreading' like a wave; it is land degradation happening mostly because of a combination of climate and human pressure. Ask: why is the edge of a desert especially vulnerable?

teach.heading: Natural cause: climate
bullets: Droughts last longer and rainfall is unreliable in semi-arid areas.
Plants die and are not replaced, leaving soil bare.
Climate change may make drought more likely in some areas.
teach.note: Link back to circulation: the Sahel sits where the rain-bearing belt moves north and south with the seasons, so a small change in its position causes drought. Distinguish between a drought (temporary) and desertification (long-term damage). Droughts begin the damage, but people's actions often make it permanent.

teach.heading: Human causes
bullets: Population growth: more people need food, fuel and land.
Overgrazing: animals strip plants and trample the soil.
Over-cultivation and removal of trees for firewood expose soil.
teach.note: Walk through each cause in a chain: more people, more animals and more farms, then plants are removed, then roots no longer hold soil, so wind and rain remove topsoil. Firewood collection is a daily need for many families without other fuel; this is why solutions must offer alternatives. Poor irrigation can also make soils salty, which we will meet in lesson 8.

teach.heading: Soil erosion cycle
bullets: Plants removed, so roots no longer bind the soil.
Wind and rain remove topsoil; less water is stored.
Fewer plants can grow, so erosion gets worse.
teach.note: Draw this as a cycle on the board: it is a positive feedback loop. Ask pupils to start at any point and explain the next. Link to the Dust Bowl only if time allows. Key exam skill: use linking words such as 'which leads to', 'so', 'therefore' to show a chain of reasoning.

practice: Sort these into natural and human causes: drought, overgrazing, firewood collection, climate change, over-cultivation.
Complete the chain: more livestock, so ... , so ... , so soil is eroded.
independent: Explain two human causes of desertification. (4 marks)
Describe how the soil erosion cycle makes desertification worse. (4 marks)
Stretch: Evaluate whether natural or human causes are more important in desertification in the Sahel. (6 marks)
exit: Name one human cause of desertification and explain it in one sentence.
lessons.homework: Draw and annotate a flow diagram showing how overgrazing leads to desertification.
lessons.send: SEND: cause and effect card sort. EAL: chains with sentence stems 'This leads to...'. Stretch: research how population growth in the Sahel affects land use.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Hot desert environments (AQA 3.1.2 The living world)
lessons.title: Reducing the risk of desertification
objectives: Describe water and soil management strategies for reducing desertification
Explain how each strategy works and why appropriate technology suits poorer areas
Evaluate and write a 6-mark answer on reducing desertification

keywords.def: simple, low-cost tools and methods that local people can make and maintain
the build-up of salt in soil, often caused by poor irrigation in hot climates
lines of stones laid along contours to slow runoff and trap water and soil
a salt-tolerant shrub planted to stabilise soil and provide fodder for animals
meeting present needs without harming the ability of future generations to meet theirs

starter: Say Bismillah. Define desertification.
Give two human causes of desertification.
Explain how soil erosion can make desertification worse.

teach.heading: Water management
bullets: Rainwater harvesting: johads and ponding banks trap rain.
Drip irrigation delivers water slowly to roots, reducing waste.
Poor irrigation causes salinisation, so efficient methods matter.
teach.note: Salinisation: in hot dry places water evaporates quickly and leaves salts behind, so heavily irrigated soil can become too salty for crops. Drip irrigation reduces evaporation and the amount of salt left in the soil. Pupils should know the connection between evaporation and salt build-up. The link to Rajasthan's johads recalls lesson 6.

teach.heading: Soil management
bullets: Stone bunds and contour traps slow runoff and trap soil.
Planting trees and shrubs such as Atriplex holds soil with roots.
Manure improves soil; crop rotation prevents over-cultivation.
teach.note: Explain that stone lines laid along the contours slow rainwater, which then soaks in rather than washing the soil away. They are cheap and can be built by villagers with local stones. Atriplex is salt-tolerant and gives animal feed. Trees also give shade and wind protection. Remind pupils of the Prophet's words recorded by al-Bukhari and Muslim: when a Muslim plants a tree or sows a crop and a person, bird or animal eats from it, it is charity (sadaqah) for him.

teach.heading: Appropriate technology
bullets: Low-cost, simple tools that local people can use and repair.
Villages use stones, manure and hand tools rather than machines.
Local ownership means projects continue after outside help ends.
teach.note: Compare with expensive solutions such as large dams and pipelines, which poorer countries may not afford or maintain. Appropriate technology is cheaper and local people are involved in the decisions. Ask pupils: why might a project fail if local people are not involved?

teach.heading: Evaluating strategies
bullets: Cheap local methods are sustainable and easy to maintain.
Large schemes need money, skills and may disturb local people.
Success depends on education, community involvement and funding.
teach.note: Model the 6-mark structure: (1) identify two strategies, (2) explain how each works, (3) compare cost and sustainability, (4) give a clear judgement. Use the plan from the Drive: a flow chart linking strategies to the problem they address, to the level of development, and the limits of each. Mark with the class and ask pupils to self-mark using the mark scheme levels.

practice: Make a flow chart linking each strategy (stone bunds, tree planting, rainwater harvesting, drip irrigation) to the cause of desertification it reduces.
Explain why Atriplex planting is useful on the edge of a desert.
independent: Explain how soil management can reduce the risk of desertification. (4 marks)
Explain why appropriate technology is suited to poorer countries. (3 marks)
Stretch: 'Water management is the most important way to reduce desertification.' How far do you agree? (6 marks)
exit: Explain how stone bunds help prevent soil erosion.
lessons.homework: Complete a 6-mark exam question on reducing the risk of desertification, using the PEE structure, and self-mark it.
